summary: This Wikipedia article defines fertilizer as any natural or synthetic material applied to soil or plant tissues to supply plant nutrients, focusing on the macronutrients nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. It traces fertilizer history from ancient manure use through 19th-century synthetic industry and the Haber process, gives production and usage statistics, and describes the nutritional role of each element and the microbiological reactions affecting nitrogen efficiency. The page also covers the environmental consequences of fertilizer use, such as water pollution, eutrophication and emissions, and mentions sustainable-agriculture alternatives. The extracted text ends partway through the microbiology section, so later sections on application, environmental effects and policy are not included.
one_line: Wikipedia overview of fertilizers: their definition, history, NPK nutrients, production statistics, and environmental effects.
key_facts: A fertilizer is any material of natural or synthetic origin applied to soil or plant tissues to supply plant nutrients.
For most modern agriculture, fertilization focuses on three main macronutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K).
John Bennet Lawes, an English entrepreneur, patented a manure formed by treating phosphates with sulfuric acid in 1842, and was the first to create the artificial manure industry.
The Haber process, invented at the beginning of the 20th century, produces ammonia from methane and molecular nitrogen from the air.
After World War II, nitrogen production plants that had ramped up for wartime bomb manufacturing were pivoted towards agriculture uses.
Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer use has risen almost 20-fold to the current rate of 100 million tonnes of nitrogen per year.
It has been estimated that almost half the people on the Earth are currently fed as a result of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer use.
The use of phosphate fertilizers increased from 9 million tonnes per year in 1960 to 40 million tonnes per year in 2000.
Agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers in 2021 was 195 million tonnes of nutrients, of which 56% was nitrogen.
Asia represented 53% of world total agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers in 2021, followed by the Americas (29%), Europe (12%), Africa (4%) and Oceania (2%).
A maize crop yielding 6–9 tonnes of grain per hectare requires 31–50 kilograms of phosphate fertilizer; soybean crops require about half, 20–25 kg per hectare.
Yara International is the world's largest producer of nitrogen-based fertilizers.
Founded in 1812, Mirat, producer of manures and fertilizers, is claimed to be the oldest industrial business in Salamanca (Spain).
The Birkeland–Eyde process fixed atmospheric nitrogen into nitric acid and was built in Rjukan and Notodden in Norway alongside large hydroelectric facilities.
Nitrogen is the most important fertilizer because it is present in proteins, DNA and chlorophyll, and atmospheric nitrogen must be converted to a fixed form to be usable by plants.
Increased nitrogen fertilizer use (800% increase between 1961 and 2019) has been a crucial component of the increased productivity of conventional food systems during the Green Revolution.
